title: Fill in the Blank
summary: The blank is usually the conclusion. Follow where the reasoning is heading, and finish it without going one step further.

slides.title: Finish the author’s thought
body: A blank after “so”, “thus” or “then” is a conclusion. A blank after “since” or “because” is a premise. Either way, it must fit exactly where the reasoning points.
The answer finishes the thought the passage set up. It doesn’t add a new idea and doesn’t claim more than the reasoning supports.
slides.callout: Read the word just before the blank. It tells you what job the missing sentence does.

slides.title: How you’ll see it
stems: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?
Which one of the following most logically completes the passage?
Which one of the following most reasonably completes the argument?

steps.label: Read the signal
steps.do: The word before the blank: therefore (conclusion), because (premise), but (contrast), for example (illustration).

steps.label: Trace the direction
steps.do: Where is the reasoning heading? Often it rejects a common view stated at the start.

steps.label: Predict
steps.do: Write the missing sentence in your own words, no stronger than the evidence.

steps.label: Match and check strength
steps.do: Pick the choice that matches; reject any that go further than the evidence.

slides.title: Worked example
slides.stimulus: Many people assume that a restaurant with long lines outside must serve excellent food. But lines also form when a restaurant is understaffed or has few tables. A long line, then, ______.
slides.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?

choices.A: does not by itself show that a restaurant's food is excellent
choices.B: is a sign that a restaurant needs to hire more staff
choices.C: shows that a restaurant's food is probably not excellent
choices.D: is more common at restaurants with few tables than at large restaurants
choices.E: tells diners nothing useful about a restaurant

steps.label: Signal
steps.note: “then” before the blank: it’s the conclusion.

steps.label: Direction
steps.note: The passage sets up a common belief (long line means great food) and then gives other causes of lines.
steps.highlight: But lines also form when a restaurant is understaffed or has few tables.

steps.label: Predict
steps.note: A long line isn’t proof of great food. No more than that.

why.A: Correct. It rejects the inference without overreaching.
why.B: Too strong: understaffing is one possible cause, not established.
why.C: Goes too far the other way: other causes don't make good food unlikely.
why.D: A comparison the passage never makes.
why.E: Extreme: a line may still tell diners something.

slides.title: Cheat card
lines: The word before the blank sets the job.
Follow the passage’s direction; it often rejects an opening claim.
Overstrong and opposite-direction choices are the usual traps.
